verses.zh: 我与眼睛立约，怎能恋恋瞻望处女呢？
verses.en: “I made a covenant with[NOTE:1] my eyes;how then could I entertain thoughts against a virgin?[NOTE:2]
notes: The idea of cutting a covenant for something may suggest a covenant that is imposed, except that this construction elsewhere argues against it (see 2 Chr 29:10).
This half-verse is the effect of the covenant. The interrogative מָה (mah) may have the force of the negative, and so be translated “not to pay attention.”

verses.zh: 从至上的　神所得之分，从至高全能者所得之业是甚么呢？
verses.en: What then would be one’s lot from God above,one’s heritage from the Almighty[NOTE:1] on high?
notes: Heb “lot of Shaddai,” which must mean “the lot from Shaddai,” a genitive of source.

verses.zh: 岂不是祸患临到不义的，灾害临到作孽的呢？
verses.en: Is it not misfortune for the unjustand disaster for those who work iniquity?

verses.zh: 神岂不是察看我的道路，数点我的脚步呢？
verses.en: Does he not see my waysand count all my steps?

verses.zh: 我若与虚谎同行，脚若追随诡诈；
verses.en: If[NOTE:1] I have walked in falsehoodand if[NOTE:2] my foot has hastened[NOTE:3] to deceit—
notes: The normal approach is to take this as the protasis, and then have it resumed in v. 7 after a parenthesis in v. 6. But some take v. 6 as the apodosis and a new protasis in v. 7.
The “if” is understood by the use of the consecutive verb.
The verbs “walk” and “hasten” (referring in the verse to the foot) are used metaphorically for the manner of life Job lived.

verses.zh: （我若被公道的天平称度，使　神可以知道我的纯正；）
verses.en: let him[NOTE:1] weigh me with honest[NOTE:2] scales;then God will discover[NOTE:3] my integrity.
notes: “God” is undoubtedly the understood subject of this jussive. However, “him” is retained in the translation at this point to avoid redundancy since “God” occurs in the second half of the verse.

The word צֶדֶךְ (tsedeq, “righteousness”) forms a fitting genitive for the scales used in trade or justice. The “scales of righteousness” are scales that conform to the standard (see the illustration in Deut 25:13-15). They must be honest scales to make just decisions.

The verb is וְיֵדַע (veyedaʿ, “and [then] he [God] will know”). The verb could also be subordinated to the preceding jussive, “so that God may know.” The meaning of “to know” here has more the idea of “to come to know; to discover.”

verses.zh: 我的脚步若偏离正路，我的心若随着我的眼目，若有玷污粘在我手上；
verses.en: If my footsteps have strayed from the way,if my heart has gone after my eyes,[NOTE:1] or if anything[NOTE:2] has defiled my hands,
notes: The meaning is “been led by what my eyes see.”

The word מֻאוּם (muʾum) could be taken in one of two ways. One reading is to represent מוּם (mum, “blemish,” see the Masorah); the other is for מְאוּמָה (meʾumah, “anything,” see the versions and the Kethib). Either reading fits the passage.

verses.zh: 就愿我所种的有别人吃，我田所产的被拔出来。
verses.en: then let me sow[NOTE:1] and let another eat,and let my crops[NOTE:2] be uprooted.
notes: The cohortative is often found in the apodosis of the conditional clause (see GKC 320 §108.f).

The word means “what sprouts up” (from יָצָא [yatsaʾ] with the sense of “sprout forth”). It could refer metaphorically to children (and so Kissane and Pope), as well as in its literal sense of crops. The latter fits here perfectly.

verses.zh: 我若受迷惑，向妇人起淫念，在邻舍的门外蹲伏，
verses.en: If my heart has been enticed by a woman,and I have lain in wait at my neighbor’s door,[NOTE:1]
notes: Gordis notes that the word פֶּתַח (petakh, “door”) has sexual connotations in rabbinic literature, based on Prov 7:6ff. (see b. Ketubbot 9b). See also the use in Song 4:12 using a synonym.

verses.zh: 就愿我的妻子给别人推磨，别人也与她同室。
verses.en: then let my wife turn the millstone[NOTE:1] for another man,and may other men commit adultery with her.[NOTE:2]
notes: Targum Job interpreted the verb טָחַן (takhan, “grind”) in a sexual sense, and this has influenced other versions and commentaries. But the literal sense fits well in this line. The idea is that she would be a slave for someone else (or someone else’s wife). The second line of the verse then might build on this to explain what kind of a slave—a concubine (see A. B. Davidson, Job, 215).

The idea is that if Job were guilty of adultery it would be an offense against the other woman’s husband, and so by talionic justice another man’s adultery with Job’s wife would be an offense against him. He is not wishing something on his wife; rather, he is simply looking at what would be offenses in kind.tn Heb “kneel down over her,” an idiom for sexual relations.

verses.zh: 因为这是大罪，是审判官当罚的罪孽。
verses.en: For I would have committed[NOTE:1] a shameful act,[NOTE:2] an iniquity to be judged.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “for that [would be].” In order to clarify the referent of “that,” which refers to v. 9 rather than v. 10, the words “I have committed” have been supplied in the translation.
The word for “shameful act” is used especially for sexual offenses (cf. Lev 18:27).

The expression עָוֹן פְּלִילִים (ʿavon pelilim) means “an iniquity of the judges.” The first word is not spelled as a construct noun, and so this has led some to treat the second word as an adjective (with enclitic mem [ם]). The sense is similar in either case, for the adjective occurs in Job 31:28 meaning “calling for judgment” (See GKC 427 §131.s).tc Some have deleted this verse as being short and irrelevant, not to mention problematic. But the difficulties are not insurmountable, and there is no reason to delete it. There is a Kethib-Qere reading in each half verse; in the first the Kethib is masculine for the subject but the Qere is feminine going with “shameless deed.” In the second colon the Kethib is the feminine agreeing with the preceding noun, but the Qere is masculine agreeing with “iniquity.”

verses.zh: 这本是火焚烧，直到毁灭，必拔除我所有的家产。
verses.en: For it is a fire that devours even to Destruction,[NOTE:1] and it would uproot[NOTE:2] all my harvest.
notes: Heb “to Abaddon.”

The verb means “to root out,” but this does not fit the parallelism with fire. Wright changed two letters and the vowels in the verb to get the root צָרַף (tsaraf, “to burn”). The NRSV has “burn to the root.”

verses.zh: 我的仆婢与我争辩的时候，我若藐视不听他们的情节；
verses.en: “If I have disregarded the right of my male servants or my female servantswhen they disputed[NOTE:1] with me,
notes: This construction is an adverbial clause using the temporal preposition, the infinitive from רִיב (riv, “contend”), and the suffix which is the subjective genitive.

verses.zh: 神兴起，我怎样行呢？他察问，我怎样回答呢？
verses.en: then what will I do when God confronts me in judgment;[NOTE:1] when he intervenes,[NOTE:2] how will I respond to him?
notes: Heb “arises.” The LXX reads “takes vengeance,” an interpretation that is somewhat correct but unnecessary. The verb “to rise” would mean “to confront in judgment.”

The verb פָּקַד (paqad) means “to visit,” but with God as the subject it means any divine intervention for blessing or cursing, anything God does that changes a person’s life. Here it is “visit to judge.”

verses.zh: 造我在腹中的，不也是造他吗？将他与我抟在腹中的岂不是一位吗？
verses.en: Did not the one who made me in the womb make them?[NOTE:1] Did not the same one form us in the womb?
notes: Heb “him,” but the plural pronoun has been used in the translation to indicate that the referent is the servants mentioned in v. 13 (since the previous “him” in v. 14 refers to God).

verses.zh: 我若不容贫寒人得其所愿，或叫寡妇眼中失望，
verses.en: If I have refused to give the poor what they desired,[NOTE:1] or caused the eyes of the widow to fail,
notes: Heb “kept the poor from [their] desire.”

verses.zh: 或独自吃我一点食物，孤儿没有与我同吃；
verses.en: if I ate my morsel of bread myself,and did not share any of it with orphans[NOTE:1]—
notes: Heb “and an orphan did not eat from it.”

verses.zh: （从幼年时孤儿与我同长，好像父子一样；我从出母腹就扶助（原文是引领）寡妇。）
verses.en: but from my youth I raised the orphan[NOTE:1] like a father,and from my mother’s womb[NOTE:2] I guided the widow[NOTE:3]—
notes: Heb “he grew up with me.” Several commentators have decided to change the pronoun to “I,” and make it causative.
The expression “from my mother’s womb” is obviously hyperbolic. It is a way of saying “all his life.”
Heb “I guided her,” referring to the widow mentioned in v. 16.

verses.zh: 我若见人因无衣死亡，或见穷乏人身无遮盖；
verses.en: if I have seen anyone about to perish for lack of clothing,or a poor man without a coat,

verses.zh: 我若不使他因我羊的毛得暖，为我祝福；
verses.en: whose heart did not bless me[NOTE:1] as he warmed himself with the fleece of my sheep,[NOTE:2]
notes: The MT has simply “if his loins did not bless me.” In the conditional clause this is another protasis. It means, “if I saw someone dying and if he did not thank me for clothing them.” It is Job’s way of saying that whenever he saw a need he met it, and he received his share of thanks—which prove his kindness. G. R. Driver has it “without his loins having blessed me,” taking “If…not” as an Aramaism, meaning “except” (AJSL 52 [1935/36]: 164f.).
This clause is interpreted here as a subordinate clause to the first half of the verse. It could also be a separate clause: “was he not warmed…?”

verses.zh: 我若在城门口见有帮助我的，举手攻击孤儿；
verses.en: if I have raised my hand[NOTE:1] to vote against the orphan,when I saw my support in the court,[NOTE:2]
notes: The expression “raised my hand” refers to a threatening manner or gesture in the court rather than a threat of physical violence in the street. Thus the words “to vote” are supplied in the translation to indicate the setting.

Heb “gate,” referring to the city gate where judicial decisions were rendered in the culture of the time. The translation uses the word “court” to indicate this to the modern reader, who might not associate a city gate complex with judicial functions.

verses.zh: 情愿我的肩头从缺盆骨脱落，我的膀臂从羊矢骨折断。
verses.en: then[NOTE:1] let my arm fall from the shoulder,[NOTE:2] let my arm be broken off at the socket.[NOTE:3]
notes: Here is the apodosis, the imprecation Job pronounces on himself if he has done any of these things just listed.

The point is that if he has raised his arm against the oppressed it should be ripped off at the joint. The MT has “let fall my shoulder [כְּתֵפִי, ketefi] from the nape of the neck [or shoulder blade (מִשִּׁכְמָה, mishikhmah)].”

The word קָנֶה (qaneh) is “reed; shaft; beam,” and here “shoulder joint.” All the commentaries try to explain how “reed” became “socket; joint.” This is the only place that it is used in such a sense. Whatever the exact explanation—and there seems to be no convincing view—the point of the verse is nonetheless clear.

verses.zh: 因　神降的灾祸使我恐惧；因他的威严，我不能妄为。
verses.en: For the calamity from God was a terror to me,[NOTE:1] and by reason of his majesty[NOTE:2] I was powerless.
notes: The LXX has “For the terror of God restrained me.” Several commentators changed it to “came upon me.” Driver had “The fear of God was burdensome.” I. Eitan suggested “The terror of God was mighty upon me” (“Two unknown verbs: etymological studies,” JBL 42 [1923]: 22-28). But the MT makes clear sense as it stands.
The form is וּמִשְּׂאֵתוֹ (umisseʾeto); the preposition is causal. The form, from the verb נָשָׂא (nasaʾ, “to raise; to lift high”), refers to God’s exalted person, his majesty (see Job 13:11).

verses.zh: 我若以黄金为指望，对精金说：你是我的倚靠；
verses.en: “If I have put my confidence in goldor said to pure gold, ‘You are my security!’

verses.zh: 我若因财物丰裕，因我手多得资财而欢喜；
verses.en: if I have rejoiced because of the extent of my wealth,or because of the great wealth my hand had gained,

verses.zh: 我若见太阳发光，明月行在空中，
verses.en: if I looked at the sun[NOTE:1] when it was shining,and the moon advancing as a precious thing,
notes: Heb “light,” but parallel to the moon it is the sun. This section speaks of false worship of the sun and the moon.

verses.zh: 心就暗暗被引诱，口便亲手；
verses.en: so that my heart was secretly enticed,and my hand threw them a kiss from my mouth,[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “and my hand kissed my mouth.” The idea should be that of “my mouth kissed my hand.” H. H. Rowley suggests that the hand was important in waving or throwing the kisses of homage to the sun and the moon, and so it receives the focus. This is the only place in the OT that refers to such a custom. Outside the Bible it was known, however.

verses.zh: 这也是审判官当罚的罪孽，又是我背弃在上的　神。
verses.en: then this[NOTE:1] also would be iniquity to be judged,[NOTE:2] for I would have been false[NOTE:3] to God above.
notes: Heb “it.”

See v. 11 for the construction. In Deut 17:2ff. false worship of heavenly bodies is a capital offense. In this passage, Job is talking about just a momentary glance at the sun or moon and the brief lapse into a pagan thought. But it is still sin.

The verb כָּחַשׁ (kakhash) in the Piel means “to deny.” The root meaning is “to deceive; to disappoint; to grow lean.” Here it means that he would have failed or proven unfaithful because his act would have been a denial of God.

verses.zh: 我若见恨我的遭报就欢喜，见他遭灾便高兴；
verses.en: If[NOTE:1] I have rejoiced over the misfortune of my enemy[NOTE:2] or exulted[NOTE:3] because calamity[NOTE:4] found him—
notes: The problem with taking this as “if,” introducing a conditional clause, is finding the apodosis, if there is one. It may be that the apodosis is understood, or summed up at the end. This is the view taken here. But R. Gordis (Job, 352) wishes to take this word as the indication of the interrogative, forming the rhetorical question to affirm he has never done this. However, in that case the parenthetical verses inserted become redundant.

The law required people to help their enemies if they could (Exod 23:4; also Prov 20:22). But often in the difficulties that ensued, they did exult over their enemies’ misfortune (Pss 54:7; 59:10 [11], etc.). But Job lived on a level of purity that few ever reach. Duhm said, “If chapter 31 is the crown of all ethical developments of the O.T., verse 29 is the jewel in that crown.”
The Hitpael of עוּר (ʿur) has the idea of “exult.”
The word is רָע (raʿ, “evil”) in the sense of anything that harms, interrupts, or destroys life.

verses.zh: （我没有容口犯罪，咒诅他的生命；）
verses.en: I[NOTE:1] have not even permitted my mouth[NOTE:2] to sinby asking[NOTE:3] for his life through a curse—
notes: This verse would then be a parenthesis in which he stops to claim his innocence.
Heb “I have not given my palate.”

The infinitive construct with the ל (lamed) preposition (“by asking”) serves in an epexegetical capacity here, explaining the verb of the first colon (“permitted…to sin”). To seek a curse on anyone would be a sin.

verses.zh: 若我帐棚的人未尝说，谁不以主人的食物吃饱呢？
verses.en: if[NOTE:1] the members of my household[NOTE:2] have never said,[NOTE:3] ‘If only there were[NOTE:4] someone who has not been satisfied from Job’s[NOTE:5] meat!’—
notes: Now Job picks up the series of clauses serving as the protasis.
Heb “the men of my tent.” In context this refers to members of Job’s household.

The line is difficult to sort out. Job is saying it is sinful “if his men have never said, ‘O that there was one who has not been satisfied from his food.’” If they never said that, it would mean there were people out there who needed to be satisfied with his food.
The optative is again expressed with “who will give?”
Heb “his”; the referent (Job) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: （从来我没有容客旅在街上住宿，却开门迎接行路的人；）
verses.en: but[NOTE:1] no stranger[NOTE:2] had to spend the night outside,for I opened my doors to the traveler[NOTE:3]—
notes: This verse forms another parenthesis. Job stops almost at every point now in the conditional clauses to affirm his purity and integrity.

Or “[resident] foreigner.” The term גֵּר (ger) refers to a foreign resident, but with different social implications in different settings. Here the “stranger” stands in need of the hospitality of lodgings.

The word in the MT, אֹרחַ (ʾorakh, “way”), is a contraction from אֹרֵחַ (ʾoreakh, “wayfarer”); thus, “traveler.” The same parallelism is found in Jer 14:8. The reading here “on/to the road” is meaningless otherwise.

verses.zh: 我若像亚当（或译：别人）遮掩我的过犯，将罪孽藏在怀中；
verses.en: if[NOTE:1] I have covered my transgressions as men do,[NOTE:2] by hiding[NOTE:3] iniquity in my heart,[NOTE:4]
notes: Now the protasis continues again.
Some commentators suggest taking the meaning here to be “as Adam,” referring to the Paradise story of the sin and denial.
The infinitive is epexegetical, explaining the first line.
The MT has “in my bosom.” This is the only place in the OT where this word is found. But its meaning is well attested from Aramaic.

verses.zh: 因惧怕大众，又因宗族藐视我使我惊恐，以致闭口无言，杜门不出；
verses.en: because I was terrified[NOTE:1] of the great multitude,[NOTE:2] and the contempt of families terrified me,so that I remained silentand would not go outdoors—
notes: Here too the verb will be the customary imperfect—it explains what he continually did in past time.
Heb “the great multitude.” But some commentators take רַבָּה (rabbah) adverbially: “greatly” (see RSV).

verses.zh: 惟愿有一位肯听我！（看哪，在这里有我所划的押，愿全能者回答我！）
verses.en: “If only I had[NOTE:1] someone to hear me!Here is my signature[NOTE:2]— let the Almighty answer me!If only I had an indictment[NOTE:3] that my accuser had written.[NOTE:4]
notes: The optative is again introduced with “who will give to me hearing me?”—“O that someone would listen to me!”

Heb “here is my ‘tav’” (הֵן תָּוִי, hen tavi). The letter ת (tav) is the last letter of the alphabet in Hebrew. In paleo-Hebrew the letter was in the form of a cross or an “X,” and so used for one making a mark or a signature. In this case Job has signed his statement and delivered it to the court—but he has yet to be charged. Kissane thought that this being the last letter of the alphabet, Job was saying, “This is my last word.” Others take the word to mean “desire”—“this is my desire, that God would answer me” (see E. F. Sutcliffe, “Notes on Job, textual and exegetical,” Bib 30 [1949]: 71-72; G. R. Driver, “Problems in Job,” AJSL 52 [1935/36]: 166; P. P. Saydon, “Philological and Textual Notes to the Maltese Translation of the Old Testament,” CBQ 23 [1961]: 252). R. Gordis (Job, 355) also argues strongly for this view.
Heb “a scroll,” in the context referring to a scroll containing the accusations of Job’s legal adversary (see the next line).
The last line is very difficult; it simply says, “a scroll [that] my [legal] adversary had written.” The simplest way to handle this is to see it as a continuation of the optative (RSV).

verses.zh: 愿那敌我者所写的状词在我这里！我必带在肩上，又绑在头上为冠冕。
verses.en: Surely[NOTE:1] I would wear it proudly[NOTE:2] on my shoulder,I would bind[NOTE:3] it on me like a crown;
notes: The clause begins with the positive oath formula, אִם־לֹא (ʾim loʾ).
The word “proudly” is not in the Hebrew text, but is implied (note the following line).
This verb is only found in Prov 6:21. But E. Dhorme (Job, 470) suggests that (with metathesis) we have a derivative מַעֲדַנּוֹת (maʿadannot, “bonds; ties”) in 38:31.

verses.zh: 我必向他述说我脚步的数目，必如君王进到他面前。
verses.en: I would give him an accounting of my steps;like a prince I would draw near to him.

verses.zh: 我若夺取田地，这地向我喊冤，犁沟一同哭泣；
verses.en: “If my land cried out against me[NOTE:1] and all its furrows wept together,
notes: Many commentators place vv. 38-40b at the end of v. 34, so that there is no return to these conditional clauses after his final appeal.

verses.zh: 我若吃地的出产不给价值，或叫原主丧命；
verses.en: if I have eaten its produce without paying,[NOTE:1] or caused the death[NOTE:2] of its owners,[NOTE:3]
notes: Some commentators have suggested that the meaning behind this is that Job might not have kept the year of release (Deut 15:1), and the law against mixing seed (Lev 19:19). But the context will make clear that the case considered is obtaining the land without paying for it and causing the death of its lawful owner (see H. H. Rowley, Job [NCBC], 206). Similar to this would be the case of Naboth’s vineyard.
Heb “without silver.”

The versions have the verb “grieved” here. The Hebrew verb means “to breathe,” but the form is Hiphil. This verb in that stem could mean something of a contemptuous gesture, like “sniff” in Mal 1:13. But with נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh) in Job 11:20 it means “to cause death,” i.e., “to cause to breathe out; to expire.” This is likely the meaning here, although it is possible that it only meant “to cause suffering” to the people.

verses.zh: 愿这地长蒺藜代替麦子，长恶草代替大麦。约伯的话说完了。
verses.en: then let thorns sprout up in place of wheat,and in place of barley, noxious weeds.”[NOTE:1] The words of Job are ended.
notes: There is some debate over the meaning of בְּעָלֶיהָ (beʿaleha), usually translated “its owners.” Dahood, following others (although without their emendations), thought it referred to “laborers” (see M. Dahood, Bib 41 [1960]: 303; idem, Bib 43 [1962]: 362).
